claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by formation of a coherent, epitaxial oxide shell.
The oxide shell suppresses elemental segregation.
The oxide shell suppresses atomic diffusion.
Suppressing segregation and diffusion preserves the nanoparticles' initial composition and crystal structure.
The initial nanoparticles have an FCC solid-solution structure.
The initial nanoparticles contain a mixture of 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metals.
CoCrFeMnNi is given as an example of the stated mixture of 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metals.
Annealing at 973 K for 24 hours in 10% H2 and 90% Ar induces formation of the coherent oxide shell.
The shell is approximately 2–5 nm thick.
The shell may consist of Cr2O3 or MnO2.
Shell-forming annealing produces a 30% increase in structural stability relative to unannealed nanoparticles.
Structural stability can be assessed by retention of the initial crystal structure and composition using XRD and EDS.
The proposed mechanism applies to nanoparticles between 10 and 50 nm.
The proposed mechanism applies at 773–1173 K for catalytic operation and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use under 10% H2 and 90% Ar at 1 atm.

contradictions.description: The material is described as mixing 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metals, but the sole example, CoCrFeMnNi, contains only first-row transition-metal elements and therefore does not instantiate the stated mixture.

Formation of an oxide shell should itself alter composition-sensitive EDS spectra, yet a 10% or greater EDS change is designated as evidence of decreased stability and falsification. The criterion could therefore classify the expected mediator as a falsifying observation.
